sum.title: The benefits of rooftop gardens
sum.label: Q1(f) Summary
sum.prompt: According to Text B, what are the benefits of rooftop gardens for cities and the people who live in them? You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible. Your summary should not be more than 120 words.

texts.title: Text B · Gardens in the Sky
paras: Look down on almost any large city from the air and you will see acres of flat grey roofs. Increasingly, though, some of those roofs are turning green. In cities from Singapore to Rotterdam, planners and residents are planting gardens on top of buildings, and the reasons go well beyond appearances.

The most obvious benefit is cooling. Dark roofs soak up the sun and release heat long after dark, which helps make city centres several degrees warmer than the countryside around them. A layer of soil and plants absorbs far less heat, so the floors below stay cooler and residents rely less on air conditioning. Plants also trap rain. During heavy storms, a green roof holds water and releases it slowly, easing the pressure on drains that might otherwise flood the streets.

There are benefits for wildlife too. Bees, butterflies and birds that have been pushed out of cities by concrete find food and shelter on rooftops, sometimes several storeys above the traffic. Some gardens grow vegetables, giving people in crowded neighbourhoods fresh food that has not travelled hundreds of kilometres.

Not everything about them is simple. A soaked garden is heavy, and older buildings may need expensive strengthening before one can be added. Maintenance costs money, and a neglected roof can quickly become an eyesore.

Yet the people who use them are often the most enthusiastic. "I came up here to water the tomatoes and ended up talking to neighbours I'd ignored for ten years," says one Rotterdam resident. Researchers report the same pattern: green roofs give people a calm place to rest, and spending time among plants is linked to lower stress.

sum.model: Rooftop gardens cool cities because plants and soil absorb much less heat than dark roofs, so the rooms beneath need less air conditioning. They store rainwater during storms and release it gradually, reducing the risk of drains overflowing and streets flooding. They give bees, butterflies and birds driven out by concrete somewhere to feed and shelter. Some grow vegetables, providing crowded areas with fresh, locally grown food. They also benefit people socially and mentally: residents meet neighbours they previously ignored, enjoy a peaceful place to relax, and feel less stressed among plants. Finally, they make dull grey skylines more attractive.

lang.title: How the writer presents the storm
lang.label: Q2(d) Language
lang.prompt: Re-read paragraphs 1 and 2 of Text C. Explain how the writer uses language to convey meaning and to create effect in these paragraphs. Choose three examples of words and phrases from each paragraph to support your answer. Your choices should include the use of imagery.

texts.title: Text C · The Storm
paras: By noon the sky over the bay had curdled into a bruised purple, and the wind began to prowl along the shoreline, rattling shutters and worrying at the loose corners of tarpaulins. Gulls hung motionless above the harbour wall, pinned in place like paper cut-outs, before the gusts tore them sideways and flung them inland. On the beach, the fishermen worked in silence, dragging their boats higher up the shingle, their faces set like stone.

Then the rain arrived, not falling but hurled, a grey wall that marched across the water and swallowed the lighthouse whole. The sea, which an hour earlier had lapped politely at the jetty, now reared and snarled, flinging white spray over the harbour wall as if it wanted to drag the whole town into its throat. Somewhere a window shattered. In the café, the lights flickered, steadied, then died, and for a moment the only sound was the storm's endless, furious roar.

lang.model:
Paragraph 1
The sky has "curdled into a bruised purple". "Curdled" suggests milk turning sour and thick, so the sky seems to be rotting, as if something has spoiled. "Bruised" connotes injury, as though the sky has already been beaten. Together they make it look sickly and hurt, warning that violence is coming.
The wind begins to "prowl" along the shoreline. This verb is used of predators hunting, so the wind is personified as a restless animal searching for prey. It makes the town seem vulnerable and builds tension.
The gulls are "pinned in place like paper cut-outs". The simile suggests they are flat, weightless and helpless, held still by the wind like decorations stuck to a wall. When they are "flung" inland, we see that even creatures of the air are powerless.
Overall, paragraph 1 creates quiet menace: the storm has not broken yet, but everything is in the grip of something dangerous and alive.

Paragraph 2
The rain is "not falling but hurled". Rain usually drops gently, but "hurled" suggests deliberate, violent throwing, as if the storm is attacking the town.
It becomes "a grey wall that marched across the water". A wall is solid and impossible to see through or escape, while "marched" evokes an army advancing in formation, relentless and organised.
The sea "swallowed the lighthouse whole". A lighthouse is a symbol of safety and guidance, so having it devoured as if by a monster suggests that nothing can protect the town now.
The contrast between the sea that "lapped politely" and the sea that "reared and snarled" shows its transformation from a tame, well-mannered presence into a vicious beast, like a dog turning on its owner.
Overall, paragraph 2 presents the storm at full strength as a monstrous, living force that overwhelms the town.

q3c.model:
I have worked on this beach for twenty years, but today I learned how little I know about the sea.

The signs were there from the morning. By noon the sky had turned a sickly purple, the colour of an old bruise, and the wind had started creeping along the shore, tugging at every loose shutter as if it were searching for a way in. Even the gulls could not fly against it; they hung still for a moment before being tossed inland like scraps of paper. Nobody needed to give an order. Together we hauled the boats as far up the beach as our backs would allow, saving our breath and our fear for later.

When the storm finally struck, it was worse than anything I have seen. The rain came at us sideways, a solid grey curtain that hid the lighthouse completely, and for a terrible moment I thought it had gone. The sea, which had been nudging the jetty as gently as a cat, rose up and roared, throwing spray right over the harbour wall. Somewhere glass shattered. I sheltered in the café with the others, and when the lights went out, nobody said a word. I am not ashamed to admit that my hands were shaking.

Tonight the wind has dropped and I am writing by candlelight. I keep thinking about how quickly the sea changed. We talk about it as if it belongs to us, but today it reminded us that we are only its guests. And yet I also saw what this town is made of: no one went home until every boat was safe. Tomorrow we will count the damage. Tomorrow we will start again.

q3a.title: Letter: the ferry skipper
q3a.label: Q3 Extended response
q3a.prompt: You are Amara's grandfather in Text A. After the final crossing, you write a letter to the town council.
bullets: what the ferry and the crossing have meant to you and your passengers over the years

texts.title: Text A · The Last Ferry
paras: Every evening at six, the old ferry Marisol left the harbour for the island, and every evening Amara's grandfather stood at the wheel. He had made the crossing for forty-one years. He knew which waves would lift the bow and which would slap the side, and he could tell from the colour of the sky whether his passengers would arrive dry.

Tonight was different. The council had announced that a new bridge would open in the spring, and the ferry would be sold for scrap. Most of the regular passengers seemed relieved: the bridge would cut their journey from forty minutes to six. Amara watched them hurry aboard, already talking about the time they would save.

Her grandfather said nothing. He checked the ropes twice, although he had never once found them loose, and he ran his thumb along the brass bell as if he were memorising its shape. When a small boy asked if he was sad, he laughed a little too loudly and said that bridges could not see dolphins.
Halfway across, he slowed the engine without explaining why. The passengers looked up from their phones. In the silver water beside them, three dolphins rose, breathed and vanished.

q3a.model:
Dear Members of the Council,

For forty-one years I have taken the Marisol across to the island every evening at six. As you prepare to open the new bridge, I would like to tell you what you are about to lose.

Of course the bridge is needed. Six minutes instead of forty is a real gift to people who are tired and want to reach home, and nobody should blame them for being relieved. But the crossing has never been just a journey. I have watched children see the sea for the first time and strangers become friends because there was nothing to do but talk. On the ferry, people slow down. On a bridge, they never will.

On our final crossing I slowed the engine halfway across. There was no explanation; there was only hope. And there they were: three dolphins rising beside us in the silver water, breathing once and disappearing. Every passenger looked up from their phone. Nobody spoke. A small boy who had asked me earlier whether I was sad pressed his face to the rail, and I knew he would remember that moment long after he had forgotten the bridge.

So I ask you not to send the Marisol for scrap. Keep her for weekend trips and school visits, for anyone who wants to see the bay slowly. I would gladly train a younger skipper, perhaps my granddaughter, who knows these waters almost as well as I do, and the ticket money could pay for her upkeep.

I have checked her ropes every evening for forty-one years. Let me check them a little longer.

Yours faithfully,
The skipper of the Marisol

dw1.title: Speech: should phones be banned?
dw1.label: Section A Directed writing
dw1.prompt: Your headteacher is considering a complete ban on mobile phones during the school day. You have been asked to give a speech to students and teachers in a school assembly.
bullets: evaluate the views expressed in both texts
give your own views, based on what you have read, about whether phones should be banned

texts.title: Text 1 · Ban phones. Completely.
paras: Walk into any classroom and watch what happens when a phone buzzes. Thirty heads turn. The lesson stops, even if only for a second, and the thread of a difficult idea snaps. At my children's school, a student survey found that seven in ten pupils check their phones during lessons. Seven in ten!

Phones do not only steal attention. They carry the playground into every corner of a child's life: the group chat that leaves you out, the photo you never agreed to, the comment that arrives at midnight. Banning phones during the school day gives young people seven hours of relief.

Some say students need phones for emergencies. Schools have telephones, and parents managed perfectly well before smartphones existed. Others say phones are useful for learning. Perhaps, but a textbook has never sent anyone a notification. If we want children who can concentrate, talk face to face and think for themselves, the answer is simple: lock the phones away.

texts.title: Text 2 · Phones are tools, not toys
paras: Every few years someone calls for a total phone ban, and every few years the same thing happens: phones disappear into pockets and bags, and students simply get better at hiding them. Bans do not teach anyone how to use technology well. They just move the problem out of sight.

Used properly, a phone is a remarkable learning tool. My students record experiments, translate texts, check facts and photograph the board instead of copying it out. When a family emergency happens, a quick message can save hours of worry.

Of course phones can distract, and online bullying is a real problem. But young people will spend the rest of their lives surrounded by screens. School is exactly the place to learn how to switch off notifications, manage time and treat each other kindly online. Teach responsible use; don't pretend the technology does not exist.

dw1.model:
Good morning, everyone.

Raise your hand if your phone has buzzed since you walked into this hall. Now keep it up if you checked it. Exactly. Our headteacher is considering a complete ban on phones during the school day, and I want to explain why a total ban would be a mistake, but why doing nothing would be a mistake too.

The writer of the first article makes powerful points. Anyone who has watched a lesson fall apart because of one notification knows the problem is real, and the idea of "seven hours of relief" from group chats and midnight comments is genuinely moving. Online bullying does follow students everywhere.

However, the evidence is weaker than it sounds. The survey comes from a single school, and glancing at a phone is not the same as losing a whole lesson. The writer claims parents "managed perfectly well" without smartphones but offers no proof. Above all, the article ignores the obvious problem: phones will simply be hidden.

The second writer, a teacher, tackles that problem head on, and I find this far more convincing. Bans, they argue, teach us nothing; they simply hide the problem instead of solving it. Crucially, they admit that phones distract and that cyberbullying is real before explaining why school is exactly where we should learn to handle both.

So what do I propose? Not a free-for-all, and not a total ban. Phones should be silent and out of sight in lessons unless a teacher asks for them. Lunchtimes could have phone-free zones. And every year group should be taught how to manage notifications and behave kindly towards each other online.

We will spend our whole lives surrounded by screens. Let us use our time here to learn to control them, rather than pretending they do not exist.

Thank you.

dw2.model:
Dear Mrs Okafor,

I am writing about your proposal to ban mobile phones during the school day. Having read arguments on both sides, I believe a ban is the right decision, although it will only work if it is introduced carefully.

The case for a ban is stronger than many students would like to admit. The first article describes how a single buzz can make "thirty heads turn", and anyone who sits in our lessons knows this is no exaggeration. More importantly, the writer points out that phones let playground conflicts follow us everywhere. Group chats that exclude people and photographs shared without permission are real problems here; seven hours away from them each day would give many students genuine relief. Is that not worth a little inconvenience?

I accept that the second writer raises fair points. Phones can be useful for recording experiments or translating texts, and families do worry about emergencies. However, these arguments are less convincing than they first appear. The school office has a telephone, and teachers could book tablets for lessons that need them. The claim that students will simply hide their phones is a reason to enforce a ban properly, not a reason to avoid one.

Where I agree with the second writer is that we need to learn to use technology responsibly. A ban during school hours does not prevent this. I would suggest that phones are handed in at registration and returned at the end of the day, and that tutor time includes lessons on managing notifications and behaving kindly online.

I hope you will consider these suggestions, and I would be happy to discuss them with the student council.

Yours sincerely,
A Year 11 student

cd1.model:
At four o'clock, the market is still roaring. Awnings of faded red and orange stretch over the narrow lane like the sails of stranded ships, and beneath them the air is thick with frying garlic, ripe mangoes and diesel. Traders bellow prices over one another until the words dissolve into a single cacophony, rising and falling like surf.

Look closer. At the spice stall, a woman scoops turmeric into paper cones, her fingertips stained a permanent gold. Pyramids of chillies glow beside sacks of cardamom so fragrant that passers-by slow down without knowing why. Across the lane, the fishmonger's ice has begun to sweat; silver bodies lie in rows, their eyes clouding, and he sluices the counter with a bucket of water that runs grey into the gutter.

By five, the light has changed. The sun slides behind the clock tower and shadows stretch across the cobbles, cool and blue. Voices drop. Someone laughs, tired and content, and a radio behind the noodle stall crackles out an old love song that nobody is listening to. The first metal shutter rattles down with a clatter that echoes off the walls, then another, and another, until the lane sounds like a giant drawing breath through its teeth.

The fruit seller is the last to pack away. He works slowly, as if reluctant to let the day go, and wraps each unsold papaya in newspaper as tenderly as if it were a sleeping child. Bruised tomatoes are left in a crate by the drain, where a thin cat appears, sniffs, and moves on, unimpressed. Pigeons strut between the empty stalls with the confidence of new owners.

Now the awnings are folded and the lane seems far too wide, a long grey corridor littered with cabbage leaves and flattened cardboard. A single bulb buzzes above the locked spice stall, and moths gather around it like late customers hoping for a bargain. The smells linger after their owners have gone: a ghost of garlic, a memory of ginger, the sweetness of fruit beginning to turn.

Tomorrow, before dawn, the shutters will rise and the roar will return. For now the market sleeps, and the only sound is the patient drip of melting ice, counting the seconds until morning.

cd2.model:
The doors of the Regal Cinema have not opened for thirty years, but the wind has found its own way in. It slips through a broken pane above the entrance and wanders the foyer, stirring drifts of dust that rise and settle like slow grey snow.

Light enters in thin blades between the boarded windows. It falls across the ticket counter, where a brass bell sits beside a faded poster of a film nobody remembers, the heroine's smile peeling away in long curls. The carpet, once a deep and confident crimson, has bleached to the colour of weak tea. Each step releases a soft, damp breath of mould, and somewhere beneath it a floorboard sighs.

Beyond the swing doors, the auditorium waits in near darkness. Rows of velvet seats slope towards the screen like the steps of a ruined amphitheatre. Some have collapsed; others still hold their shape, their arms worn smooth by thousands of elbows, as if the audience left a moment ago. In the front row a single seat is folded down, as though someone is still waiting for the film to begin. The screen hangs in tatters, a huge pale sail torn by damp, and behind it pigeons have built an untidy kingdom of twigs and feathers. When one shifts, the beat of its wings echoes around the cavernous room like sudden applause.

It is the silence that is hardest to bear. In a room built for gasps and laughter, there is only one sound left: the tick of water dripping from the ceiling into a rusted bucket that someone placed there long ago and never came back to empty. The air smells of wet plaster and old popcorn oil, a sour sweetness that clings to the back of the throat.

High at the back, the projection window is still intact. Through it, dust drifts in a beam of sunlight like a film waiting to be shown. For a moment it is almost possible to believe the projector will flicker into life, that music will swell and the darkness will fill with faces turned upwards, lit silver and gold.

Then a cloud passes over the sun. The beam fades. The Regal returns to its long, patient sleep, and the wind, bored, slips back out through the broken pane.

cd3.model:
At half past five, the station belongs to the pigeons. They patrol the empty platform in twos and threes, heads bobbing, inspecting the yellow line as if it were their own invention. The departure board flickers green in the gloom, its letters clicking over one by one with nobody to read them.

The air is cold enough to sting. It smells of metal and damp concrete, with a faint, warm hint of bread from the kiosk, where the shutter is half raised and a young man yawns as he lines up paper cups in perfect rows. Under the roof a loose sheet of plastic flaps and settles, flaps and settles, like a slow heartbeat. Otherwise there is nothing: no footsteps, no voices, no trains.

A cleaner moves along the platform with a wide broom, pushing a small wave of crisp packets ahead of her. She hums an old tune, and the sound carries much further than it should across the hushed tracks. Beyond the glass canopy the sky is turning from ink to pale lilac, and the rails gleam like two silver threads running into the morning.

By eight o'clock, the station is unrecognisable.

The pigeons have retreated to the girders; below them, a tide of commuters surges through the barriers: suits and school uniforms, headphones and briefcases, a toddler perched on her father's shoulders like a queen surveying her kingdom. Footsteps drum on the stairs. The announcements, which earlier echoed politely into silence, now compete with a hundred conversations and the shriek of brakes as a train slides in, already full, its windows fogged with breath.

The kiosk has become a battleground. The young man, wide awake now, slams coffee after coffee onto the counter while the queue snakes back past the timetable. The smell of bread has been swallowed by perfume, warm rubber and the sharp tang of the city waking up.

The doors open. Bodies pour out and bodies pour in, and for a few seconds the platform empties as quickly as it filled. Then the whistle blows, the train pulls away, and a single pigeon drops from the girders to inspect the yellow line again, as if nothing has happened at all.

cd4.model:
The kitchen is the beating heart of my grandmother's house, and on the first Sunday of the holidays it is working overtime.

Steam rises from three pots at once, fogging the window above the sink so that the garden becomes a soft green blur. The air is heavy with cumin, frying onions and the scorched sweetness of something left in the oven a minute too long. Nobody minds; my grandmother stands at the centre of it all, small and unhurried, stirring with a wooden spoon worn pale at the edges and giving instructions in a voice so quiet that everyone has to lean in to hear.

Around her, the family orbits. My uncle, enormous and cheerful, has been trusted with the tomatoes and chops them with the solemn concentration of a surgeon. Two of my aunts argue happily about whose turn it was to bring dessert, their bangles chiming like tiny bells. Under the table, the youngest cousins have built a fort from chair legs and a tablecloth, and every so often a small hand reaches up to steal an olive.

In the living room, the television murmurs to itself, ignored. My grandfather has fallen asleep in his armchair with a newspaper tented over his chest, rising and falling with each gentle snore. On the mantelpiece, photographs in mismatched frames watch over us: weddings, graduations, a black-and-white couple squinting into the sun on a beach decades ago. Some of those faces are at the table today. Some are not, but somehow they are here too.

When the food arrives, the noise doubles. Plates clatter, chairs scrape and three conversations collide in the middle of the table. Rice is passed from hand to hand like a precious parcel. Someone knocks over a glass, and the laughter is so loud that my grandfather wakes with a start and asks if he has missed anything.

Later, when the dishes are stacked and the light has turned golden, the house grows quiet. Cousins sprawl across the carpet, too full to move, and someone starts a sleepy argument about a board game. My grandmother sits at last, hands folded, watching us with the calm satisfaction of someone who has gathered everything she loves into one warm, crowded room.

cn1.model:
The key arrived on a Tuesday, in an envelope with no stamp and no name, just our address in shaky blue ink.

It was old and heavy, black iron longer than my hand, its teeth worn smooth. A paper tag hung from it on faded string. On the tag, someone had written a single word: Remember.

"Junk," said Mum, but she turned it over twice before handing it back, and I saw her jaw tighten.

For a week I carried it everywhere. I tried it in every lock I could find: the shed, the garage, the tin box under Mum's bed where she kept papers she never let me read. Nothing fitted. At night it lay on my bedside table, catching the street light, while I wondered whose hand had written that word.

It was Gran who recognised it. We were visiting her at the care home and I was turning the key between my fingers. She stopped mid-sentence. Her eyes, which these days drifted like boats without anchors, found mine and held them.

"Where did you get that?" she whispered. "That opens the blue house on Harbour Lane. Your grandfather's workshop."

Mum went still. My grandfather had walked out when she was a baby. That was all anyone ever said about him, and they rarely said it.

On Saturday we drove to Harbour Lane in silence. The house was squeezed between a launderette and a phone shop, its paint faded to the colour of a winter sky. The key turned stiffly, resisted, then gave.

Dust lay over everything like a sheet. Beneath it were shelves of tiny wooden boats, hundreds of them, each carved and painted by hand, each with a name on its side. Every name was Mum's.

On the workbench, beside a half-finished hull, lay a letter addressed to her, sealed and never sent. She read it standing in the doorway. When she finally looked up, her eyes were wet.

"He didn't leave because of me," she said. "He was ill. He was trying to come back."

We never found out who posted the key. But that evening Mum placed the smallest boat on our kitchen windowsill, where the light could find it.

cn2.model:
Nobody else had noticed the light in the window.

Every evening the number 12 bus crawled past Carlton Tower, and every evening I pressed my forehead to the glass and counted the floors. Fourteen storeys of dark windows, boarded and blind. The council had emptied the building in the spring. A yellow sign on the fence announced the demolition date in letters a metre high: Monday.

But on the eleventh floor, third window from the left, a small orange light was glowing.

On Thursday it was there again. On Friday it flickered, as if someone had walked in front of it. I looked around the bus. Nobody else had seen.

On Saturday I stepped off the bus two stops early.

The fence had a gap where the wire had been peeled back. My heart was hammering so hard I could feel it in my throat. The stairwell smelled of damp and pigeons, and every step echoed upwards into the dark. By the eleventh floor I could hear music: an old song, crackling, the kind my grandmother used to hum.

The door of flat 114 was open a crack.

"Hello?" My voice came out smaller than I meant it to.

The music stopped. Footsteps shuffled. The door swung open, and an elderly man in a cardigan peered at me over his glasses.

"You're not from the council," he said.

His name was Mr Adeyemi, and he had lived in flat 114 for forty years. His late wife had planted the balcony garden in their first summer: geraniums, tomatoes, a lemon tree in a cracked blue pot. He had moved to his new flat across town, but he could not carry the plants, so every evening he came back to water them, sitting with a lamp and the radio until dark.

"They knock it down on Monday," I said.

He looked at the lemon tree. "I know."

On Sunday I came back with my brother, my cousin and three borrowed shopping trolleys. It took us six trips and the whole afternoon.

Now, when the number 12 passes the empty space where Carlton Tower stood, I look across the river instead. On the fourth floor of a newer building, a small orange light glows among the leaves.

cn3.model:
The lifeguard was waving at me. I was sure of it.

It was the last afternoon of our holiday and the beach was almost empty. Mum was dozing under the umbrella, my little sister Noor was burying her own feet, and I was waist-deep in water so clear I could see my toes. Beyond the rocks, the waves were bigger, glassy and green. That was where I wanted to be.

On the tall white chair, the lifeguard stood up. She lifted both arms above her head and swept them from side to side.

I grinned, waved back, and swam towards the rocks.

At first it was easy. Too easy. The water carried me as if it wanted me out there too, and in a minute I was further out than I had meant to go in five. When I turned, the umbrella was a tiny red dot. I started to swim back.

I did not move.

I kicked harder. My arms churned. The beach stayed exactly where it was, then slowly slid further away. The water around me was strangely smooth, a dark channel between the breaking waves, pulling me out like a conveyor belt.

Panic arrived all at once. Salt filled my mouth. I could hear my own breathing, ragged and loud, and nothing else. My legs were turning to stone.

Swim sideways. The words surfaced from somewhere: a poster in the changing room, an assembly I had barely listened to. Don't fight it. Swim along the beach.

So I turned. Stroke after stroke, parallel to the shore; then a wave lifted me and pushed me forward instead of back. Was it working?

The lifeguard reached me as my knees scraped sand. She dragged me into the shallows, gasping, a long red cut down her shin where the rocks had caught her.

"I was waving," she panted, "to tell you to come back."

I looked at her leg, at the blood threading into the foam, at Mum sprinting down the beach with Noor in her arms, and I could not say anything at all.

Nobody shouted at me. That was the worst part. Mum just held me so tightly that I could feel her shaking.

Now, whenever someone waves at me from a distance, I stop. I look. And I make sure I understand.

cn4.model:
The plan was simple: the 8:14 train to the city, the museum by ten, lunch on the steps and home by four. Ms Rahman had written it on the board in green pen and made us copy it into our planners. I had copied it. I had not read it.

Which is why, at half past ten, I woke in an empty carriage with my cheek stuck to the window and no idea where I was.

Outside, instead of the grey towers of the city, there was a tiny station with a single bench, a hanging basket of drooping flowers and, beyond the fence, the sea.

Stumbling onto the platform, I heard the doors hiss shut behind me. The train slid away. The sign above the bench said Port Ellin. I had never heard of it.

My phone was dead. Of course it was. I had spent the journey playing games instead of listening to Josh explain, for the third time, which stop we needed.

For a moment I just stood there while a gull screamed at me from the roof. My stomach felt hollow. Somewhere in the city, thirty students were filing into a museum, and one empty seat was about to be noticed. Ms Rahman's face swam into my mind: pale, then crimson.

The ticket office was closed. The next train back was at 1:40. Down the hill I went, into the town, past a bakery that smelled of warm sugar, until I found a café with a handwritten sign: Phone charging, ask inside.

The woman behind the counter took one look at me and put the kettle on. While my phone charged, she rang the school, then the museum, then my mum, speaking so calmly that it seemed lost teenagers arrived in her café every week. Perhaps they did.

When Ms Rahman finally called, she did not shout. She let out a long breath that crackled down the line and said, "Stay exactly where you are."

So I did, settling by the window with a hot chocolate and a slice of lemon cake the woman refused to let me pay for, watching fishing boats nod in the harbour. Something strange had happened; I was not frightened any more.

I never saw the museum. But I still keep the café's receipt folded inside my planner, next to the plan I didn't read.

sumB.title: The problems of light at night
sumB.label: Q1(f) Summary
sumB.prompt: According to Text B, what problems are caused by artificial light at night? You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible. Your summary should not be more than 120 words.

texts.title: Text B · Lights Out
paras: A century ago, almost anyone could step outside on a clear night and see the Milky Way. Today around a third of humanity cannot, because the glow of streetlights, advertising screens and floodlit buildings drowns out the stars. Astronomers were the first to complain, but scientists are discovering that the loss of darkness affects far more than the view.

For wildlife, night-time light can be deadly. Newly hatched sea turtles find the ocean by heading towards the brightest horizon, which used to be moonlight on the water; now many crawl inland towards hotels and roads. Migrating birds, which navigate partly by the stars, become disorientated by lit skyscrapers and circle them until they are exhausted, or fly straight into the glass. Moths and other insects gather around lamps in their millions instead of feeding and pollinating plants, and the bats and birds that depend on those insects go hungry.

People are affected too. Our bodies run on an internal clock that expects darkness at night. Bright light, especially the blue-white light of modern LEDs and screens, suppresses melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy. Studies have linked poor sleep caused by light at night to tiredness, weaker concentration and, over many years, a higher risk of some illnesses. Light shining into bedrooms from outside can also make it harder for children to settle.

There is a financial cost as well. Much outdoor lighting points sideways or upwards, lighting the sky rather than the ground, so a large share of the electricity it uses is simply wasted. That waste also adds to carbon emissions.

The encouraging news is that light pollution is one of the easiest environmental problems to fix. Shielded lamps that point downwards, warmer colours, timers and motion sensors can cut the glow dramatically without making streets less safe. Some towns have already been named dark sky places, and visitors now travel to them just to see the stars.

sumB.model: Artificial light at night hides the stars from about a third of people. It also harms wildlife: young turtles crawl towards roads rather than the sea, migrating birds become confused and either circle lit towers until exhausted or hit the windows, and insects swarm around lamps instead of feeding and pollinating, which leaves bats and birds that eat them short of food. In people, bright light, particularly from LEDs and screens, reduces the hormone that brings sleep, so they rest badly, feel tired and concentrate less, with a possible long-term risk to health; children also struggle to settle. Finally, badly aimed lights waste electricity and money and increase carbon emissions.

langB.title: How the writer presents the glacier
langB.label: Q2(d) Language
langB.prompt: Re-read paragraphs 1 and 2 of Text C. Explain how the writer uses language to convey meaning and to create effect in these paragraphs. Choose three examples of words and phrases from each paragraph to support your answer. Your choices should include the use of imagery.

texts.title: Text C · The Glacier
paras: The path to the glacier climbed through a valley of grey rubble, as if a giant had emptied his pockets and walked away. Every few hundred metres a small signpost marked where the ice had reached in a particular year: 1950, 1980, 2005. The posts were absurdly far apart. By the time we reached the last one, my legs ached and the air had turned thin and sharp, scrubbed clean of every smell except wet stone. Then we rounded a ridge and the glacier was there, filling the valley's throat: a vast frozen river, scarred and ribbed, its surface the dirty white of an old bandage.

Up close it was not silent at all. It ticked, dripped, sighed. Somewhere deep inside, water was running in hidden tunnels, a constant hurried gurgle like a kettle that could never quite boil. Our guide knelt and laid her palm flat on the ice, the way you might touch the forehead of someone with a fever. Where the glacier ended, it did not stop so much as collapse: towers of blue ice leaned over a milky lake, cracked through with veins of light. While we watched, a slab the size of a house shivered, groaned, and slid into the water with a roar that echoed off the cliffs for a long time afterwards. Nobody spoke. The guide said that when she was a child, the lake had not existed.

Appropriate choices from both paragraphs, including some imagery. Meanings and effects are explained clearly and mostly precisely, with some exploration of connotations.
A reasonable selection. Explanations are general or partly accurate; effects are identified but not always explained; imagery is handled only partly.

langB.model:
Paragraph 1
The path climbs through "grey rubble, as if a giant had emptied his pockets and walked away". "Rubble" suggests the broken remains of something destroyed, and the simile of a careless giant makes the destruction seem huge and thoughtless; "walked away" hints that nobody has taken responsibility for the damage.
The signposts are "absurdly far apart". "Absurdly" conveys the writer's disbelief: the posts become a ruler measuring how fast the ice has vanished, and the distance makes the loss shocking.
The glacier fills "the valley's throat" and its surface is "the dirty white of an old bandage". The metaphor turns the valley into a body, while "bandage" connotes a wound, and "dirty" and "old" suggest the injury has been left untreated. The glacier seems hurt rather than majestic.
Overall, paragraph 1 presents a damaged landscape in which the glacier is already wounded.

Paragraph 2
The glacier "ticked, dripped, sighed". The list of verbs makes it sound alive, while "ticked" suggests a clock counting down and "sighed" adds weariness, as though it knows it is dying.
The meltwater is "a constant hurried gurgle like a kettle that could never quite boil". The simile links the glacier to heat, and "hurried" and "constant" suggest melting that cannot be stopped.
The guide touches the ice like "the forehead of someone with a fever". The simile makes the glacier a sick patient, and "fever" connotes dangerous heat, linking to a warming climate.
Finally the slab "shivered, groaned, and slid" into the lake. These verbs personify it as a creature in pain, and its "roar" echoing for a long time suggests a death that cannot be undone.
Overall, paragraph 2 develops the image of illness into the glacier's final collapse, leaving the reader with a sense of grief and loss.

q3B.model:
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the valley.

Most of you walked up here this morning, so you already know the path: grey, broken stone, mile after mile of it, with those little signposts along the way. Did you look at the dates? Every post marks where the ice once reached. When I was your age, the walk from the car park to the glacier took twenty minutes. Today it takes nearly two hours, and the air at the top is so thin and clean that you can taste the rock.

When you finally see the glacier, you might expect silence. Instead it ticks and drips and sighs. You can hear water rushing through tunnels inside it, and at the front the ice does not end neatly; it breaks apart in blue towers that lean over a pale lake. Last week I watched a block the size of a house groan and slide into that water. I have spent my whole life on this ice, and I still could not speak.

So what is the glacier telling us? Those posts are a timeline. The ice is not just shrinking; it is shrinking faster every decade, because the world is warming. The lake below it did not exist when I was a child. Glaciers like this one store water that towns and farms depend on in summer, so this is not only a beautiful place disappearing. It is a warning.

You might think that nothing you do could matter to something this enormous. It does. The way you travel, the energy your homes use, what you buy and, above all, what you say to the people who make decisions all add up. You are the generation who will live with the results, so you have every right to demand change.

When you walk back down that path today, read the signposts again. Then decide where you want the next one to stand. Thank you.

dwB.title: Article: should school start later?
dwB.label: Section A Directed writing
dwB.prompt: Your school is considering starting the school day one hour later. Write an article for your school magazine giving your views.
bullets: evaluate the views given in both texts
give your own views, based on what you have read, about whether the school day should start later

texts.title: Text 1 · Let teenagers sleep
paras: Every morning, millions of teenagers are dragged out of bed in the middle of their biological night. This is not laziness. During adolescence the body clock shifts: the sleep hormone melatonin is released around two hours later than in childhood, so most teenagers simply cannot fall asleep before eleven. If school starts at eight, they lose sleep every single day.

The evidence from schools that have changed is striking. When one group of schools moved the start of the day from 7:50 to 8:45, students slept almost an hour longer, attendance rose and grades in first-period lessons improved. Car accidents involving teenage drivers fell. Students reported feeling less anxious and more motivated.

Critics worry about buses, sports practice and parents' working hours. These are real problems, but they are problems of organisation, not of biology. We redesign timetables all the time; we cannot redesign the adolescent brain. A later start is one of the cheapest, simplest ways to improve young people's health and learning.

texts.title: Text 2 · Why we are keeping our timetable
paras: Dear parents and carers, several of you have asked whether we will follow other schools and start the day an hour later. I understand the appeal. Nobody enjoys a dark winter morning, and I have read the research on teenage sleep with interest. But I want to explain why we are not planning to change.

First, a later start means a later finish. Many of our students look after younger brothers and sisters after school, have part-time jobs or travel long distances on buses that run to fixed timetables. Finishing at 4:30 would make their afternoons harder, not easier, and sports fixtures against other schools would become almost impossible in winter.

Second, I am not convinced that a later start automatically means more sleep. Some studies suggest that teenagers simply go to bed later when they know they can get up later, especially if they are on their phones until midnight.

Instead, we will work with students on sleep habits: putting phones away an hour before bed, keeping regular bedtimes, and starting the day with a short, calm tutor period rather than a test. Small changes at home may achieve more than a big change to the timetable.
